exit_trigger: Franchise test fails: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years; Reported negative annual operating cash flow, a sign of management failure; Price above 1.5x owner-earnings intrinsic value; Evidence that clients are shifting work away from Accenture to automation and the firm lacks pricing power; Evidence of management dishonesty or value-destroying acquisitions
rationale: We own three shares of Accenture, bought a day ago at $251.845, and they are down 3.55% since. That is noise, and a price decline is never a reason to sell a business whose economics are intact. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 26.9% and debt-to-equity of 0.32. It also shows a reported margin of safety of 45.5% against an owner-earnings DCF value of $437.57 a share, though that DCF leans on an 8% growth cap and a 5% discount rate. My doubt is the moat: switching costs in consulting are real but softer than Coca-Cola's brand, and a services business that must keep rebuilding its edge against technological change is not a franchise I can underwrite for decades. So I keep the position, I don't add to it yet, and I'd want to read the earnings history and management record before I got excited.

exit_trigger: ROE falling below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years (franchise test fails); Negative annual operating cash flow in the newest five fiscal years; Price above 1.5x the owner-earnings intrinsic value on a persistent basis; Evidence of lost pricing power: sustained discounting, falling customer retention or shrinking market share; Evidence of dishonest or value-destroying management behavior
rationale: I own this one, and I'm not going to sell a business with a 5-year average ROE of 34.6% and a reported debt-to-equity of 0.0 because the price is down 16.68% since August. Price declines don't trigger a sale; moat erosion does, and nothing in this snapshot shows that. The owner-earnings DCF says $363 a share against a $106.96 price, but that rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I wouldn't bet the farm on a number that generous. My real worry is that apparel can be fashion-driven, and fashion-driven brands must be rebuilt every few years, so I can't extend full conviction. I'll keep the shares, own them for the business and not the quote, and add only if I can confirm the brand's pricing power still holds.

exit_trigger: Evidence that the switching-cost moat is eroding, such as ROE falling below 15% in a meaningful share of years; Reported negative annual operating cash flow, a sign of management or business failure; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Management capital allocation that destroys value, such as expensive acquisitions or buybacks at peak prices
rationale: I don't own Adobe, and the numbers on the page are tempting: a 5-year average ROE of 40.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a price of $236.96 against a DCF value of $467.50, which is a 49.3% margin of safety. But that DCF assumes 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and it only means something if I'm confident the franchise looks the same ten years from now. Creative software is an industry where the tools themselves may be rebuilt by new technology, and a moat that has to be rebuilt continuously is no moat at all. The snapshot also doesn't give me ten years of earnings history, management tenure, ROIC or the Treasury yield, so I can't finish my homework. I'll keep it on the list and wait for evidence that the switching costs hold, rather than buy on a cheap-looking number.

rationale: I own this one, and the numbers I can see give me no reason to sell. The shares are down about 2% since August, which means nothing to me; a price decline with the thesis intact is not a sell signal. I will keep what I own, but I need evidence on earnings consistency and management before I add to it.

exit_trigger: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years, signalling moat erosion; Negative annual operating cash flow, a sign of management or execution failure; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Loss of a major nuclear shipbuilding program or a shift in Navy procurement that weakens the industrial-base moat
rationale: I don't own this one, and I'm not ready to. A builder of warships for a single customer, the U.S. Navy, has a real barrier to entry, because almost nobody else can build these vessels. But a barrier to entry is not the same as pricing power. When your one buyer sets the terms, the moat protects your existence more than it protects your returns. The model shows a wide discount, price near $297 against about $559 of estimated value, but that value leans on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I distrust a margin of safety that comes mostly from generous assumptions. Five-year average ROE of 15.3% and debt-to-equity of 0.49 clear my bars by a whisker, not comfortably. I also can't verify ten years of earnings, CEO tenure, or the Treasury yield from this snapshot, so I'll wait.
